title: Use a Short Timebox for a Rough First Pass
subtitle: Quick Thinking with Tight Deadlines
description: Give a low-risk task a shorter-than-usual timebox, define what a useful first pass must contain, and reduce scope instead of pretending you can preserve everything by working faster.

lifeOsSource.hack: Choose a low-risk task, set a shorter timebox for a rough first pass, define what must be present at the end, and cut optional scope rather than rushing important quality checks.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Pick a low-risk task where an imperfect first pass is useful. Set a short timebox, define the minimum useful output, and decide what you will leave for later. Stop or reassess when the timebox ends.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Did the timebox help me make useful scope decisions, and what should be improved before this work is actually finished or shared?

faq.question: Does the timebox need to be 30 minutes?
faq.answer: No. Thirty minutes is only an example. Choose a shorter-than-usual window that still gives you enough time to produce a useful first pass.

faq.question: What kinds of tasks fit this approach?
faq.answer: Use it for reversible first drafts, outlines, sketches, planning, or early analysis. Avoid using artificial time pressure for safety-critical, legal, financial, medical, or other work where errors are costly.

faq.question: What if quality drops too much?
faq.answer: Reduce scope rather than lowering essential standards. Keep the core accurate and useful, then schedule a separate revision if the work needs polish or verification.

intro.html: A short timebox can help when a task is expanding because you have not decided what the first useful version actually needs. The aim is not to work at unsafe speed. It is to force a scope decision and create an earlier draft you can review.

sections.title: 1. Choose a low-risk task
sections.html: Pick something where a rough first pass has value: an outline, brief, sketch, draft email, slide structure, or list of options. Do not manufacture urgency for work where accuracy or safety needs more time.

sections.title: 2. Define the minimum useful output
sections.html: Before starting, write what must exist at the end. For example: a one-page outline with the decision, three supporting points, and open questions. This gives the timebox something concrete to protect.

sections.title: 3. Decide what can wait
sections.html: Remove optional formatting, extra examples, polish, or secondary sections from the first pass. Keep factual checks and any requirement that makes the output safe or understandable.

sections.title: 4. Work to the boundary
sections.html: Use the timebox as a stopping point for the first pass. If you get stuck, simplify the output instead of silently extending the scope. If the task turns out to be larger than expected, record what remains.

sections.title: 5. Review before sharing
sections.html: A timeboxed draft is not automatically finished work. Check accuracy, missing context, tone, and any quality requirement that matters before sending or publishing it.

sections.title: 6. Decide whether the constraint helped
sections.html: Ask whether the shorter window improved decisions or merely created stress. Keep the method for tasks where it produces a useful first pass without hiding important work.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace an inherited deadline-sprint article containing fabricated completion rates, internal-pilot results, unsupported creativity claims and rigid timing rules with a low-risk timeboxing protocol focused on scope decisions.
